claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment are prone to corrosion during exposure to molten aluminum.
Reactive sputtering can deposit a dense, stable CrN film on the surface of a component.
A dense CrN coating will remain intact and adherent during prolonged service at hot-dip aluminum-plating temperatures.
CrN acts as a diffusion barrier against penetration by molten aluminum.
Blocking or retarding molten-aluminum penetration limits corrosive interactions at the boride surface.
Sputter-deposited CrN improves the wear and corrosion resistance of conventional stainless steel.
A CrN film on 316 stainless steel beneficially affects friction behavior in NaCl solution and high-temperature environments up to 550 °C.
A CrN coating can remain relatively stable during ball-on-plate tribocorrosion testing under various applied potentials.
Reactive-sputtered CrN has proven corrosion-resistance benefits on medium-entropy alloys.
CrN-coated boride-based components will have a significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate than uncoated boride-based components.
CrN-coated boride-based components will exhibit less weight loss than uncoated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
CrN-coated boride-based components will exhibit diminished pit formation and improved surface integrity relative to uncoated components.
The protective effect should persist while the CrN film remains intact and is not mechanically compromised.
Temperatures well beyond the tested hot-dip plating range may limit the coating's protective effect.
Extreme mechanical wear or unforeseen chemical interactions may limit the CrN coating's protective capability.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement for CrN-coated boride-based components in molten aluminum is not yet established.
